summary: Specifies how members of the IAB and IESG, some IETF Trust trustees, and some IETF LLC directors are selected, confirmed, and recalled through the Nominating and Recall Committees. It is based on RFC 7437 with only the updates required by IASA 2.0, and it obsoletes RFC 7437 and RFC 8318.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook for picking and removing IETF leaders, using a committee of volunteers, like how a class might choose helpers.

how many volunteers are on the nomcom
subtitle: How the IETF picks, confirms and removes its leaders: a random committee of volunteers, a confirming body for each seat, and a petition-driven recall.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs a fair, repeatable way to fill and, when needed, vacate seats on the IAB, the IESG, the IETF Trust and the IETF LLC Board, without any one group controlling the outcome.
tldr.mechanism: A Nominating Committee (NomCom) of 10 randomly chosen volunteers selects candidates for the open seats, a confirming body approves or rejects them, and a separate recall committee can remove a sitting member after a petition.
tldr.outcome: This revision of RFC 7437 changes only what IASA 2.0 required, replacing the IAOC with the IETF LLC and adding the NomCom-appointed IETF Trust Trustees. It has since been updated by RFC 9389.

facts.label: Volunteer eligibility
facts.value: At least 3 of the last 5 IETF meetings

today: RFC 8713 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 10) that obsoletes RFC 7437 and RFC 8318, and it has been updated by RFC 9389.

sections.title: Why This Process Exists
sections.content:
RFC 8713 is a complete written specification of how members of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), some Trustees of the IETF Trust, and some Directors of the IETF Administration LLC (IETF LLC) are selected, confirmed and recalled. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 10).

It is a revision of RFC 7437, which was in turn based on RFC 3777. The revision addresses only the changes needed for IASA 2.0, the new IETF administrative structure of RFC 8711 built around the IETF LLC. Any other changes are left to future documents. It obsoletes RFC 7437 and RFC 8318.

Two assumptions carry over: the IRTF and IRSG are not part of this process, and the organization of the IESG itself is not covered. Time frames are expressed relative to the three yearly IETF meetings, called the First, Second and Third IETF.
sections.eli5: This is the rulebook for choosing the grown-ups who steer the IETF. It was updated because the IETF changed how it runs its office work.

sections.title: The Annual Cycle
sections.content:
The annual process is due to complete within seven months, one month before the Friday of the week before the First IETF. It officially begins when the committee Chair is announced and ends when all confirmed candidates have been announced. It has three parts: selecting and organizing the NomCom members, having the NomCom select candidates, and having the candidates confirmed. An extra month is held in reserve before the new terms begin, to absorb unusual circumstances.

Each year the NomCom reviews about half of the IESG and IAB seats, one IETF Trust seat and one IETF LLC Director seat. The NomCom does not pick which seats are open; it is told which positions to review and given a short summary of the expertise wanted. Incumbents must tell the NomCom if they wish to be nominated, and length of service may be one criterion for judging an incumbent. A superior candidate is one the NomCom believes would improve or enhance the body they join.

Confirmed IESG and IAB members are expected to serve at least two years. Confirmed IETF LLC Directors and IETF Trust Trustees are expected to serve at least three years, unless a shorter term is used for initial staggered appointments. Terms begin during the First IETF meeting. Mid-term vacancies are filled by the same rules, but the work is due within six weeks, the confirming body has two weeks to reject a candidate, and the new term is the remainder of the old one (or that remainder plus a full term if less than a year remains).
sections.eli5: Every year, half of the helper jobs come up for a new choice. Everyone follows a calendar so the new helpers are ready when the big meeting starts.

sections.title: Advice and Consent
sections.content:
Unless stated otherwise, the process uses an advice and consent model. The chairs of the IESG, IAB, IETF Trust and IETF LLC Board each tell the NomCom which of their positions are up for review, along with the expertise they want. The NomCom selects candidates according to its understanding of the IETF community's consensus on the qualifications needed and advises each confirming body of its candidates, giving a single candidate per open position and testifying how that person meets the qualifications.

A confirming body may consent to some, all or none of the candidates. If it rejects any, it should talk to the NomCom about why, and the NomCom must select alternates. If a confirming body has no specific decision rule, confirming a candidate should require at least one-half of its sitting members to agree. Any candidate not confirmed under the rule is rejected.

Confidentiality is a core rule. All deliberations and supporting information about specific nominees, candidates and confirmed candidates are confidential. Only the list of nominees willing to be considered is not confidential, and the NomCom may choose to publish it to gather community feedback. Nominees should not encourage public statements of support, and the community should not post support or non-support publicly.
sections.eli5: The committee suggests a name, and a separate group must say yes before the person gets the job. Everyone keeps the discussions secret so nobody gets embarrassed.

sections.title: Who Sits on the NomCom
sections.content:
The NomCom has at least a Chair, 10 voting volunteers, two liaisons and an advisor. Only the 10 voting volunteers vote on candidate selection. The Chair, liaisons and advisors vote on other matters unless the document says otherwise. The Chair is appointed by the Internet Society President and must meet the same requirements as a voting volunteer. The IAB and IESG each appoint a liaison from their sitting members, and the Internet Society Board of Trustees, the IETF Trust and the IETF LLC Board may each appoint one at their discretion. The prior year's Chair serves as an advisor, and the committee may add more advisors or liaisons by its voting mechanism.

To volunteer, a person must have attended at least three of the last five IETF meetings. The Internet Society Board of Trustees, IETF Trust, IETF LLC Board, IAB and IESG members (including ex officio ones) and IETF LLC employees or contractors may not volunteer as voting members.

A NomCom term is expected to be 15 months. It begins when the members are announced and ends at the Third IETF after the next NomCom's term begins, so consecutive terms overlap by about three months. During the overlap, mid-term vacancies go to the prior year's NomCom.
sections.eli5: The committee is ten volunteers who get to vote, plus a few helpers from other groups who watch and give advice but do not vote on who gets picked.

sections.title: Picking Members and Nominees
sections.content:
The Chair announces the list of open positions and a call for volunteers that stays open for at least 30 days. Before the draw, the Chair announces the pool of volunteers and the selection method at least one week ahead. The method must depend on random data not known until the day of the draw, must be independently verifiable, fair (each eligible volunteer equally likely to be selected) and unbiased (nobody can influence the outcome), and repeatable so that unavailable volunteers can be replaced. RFC 3797 describes one possible method.

No more than two volunteers with the same primary affiliation may be selected. The members are announced twice, with at least a one-week challenge period in between. A challenge goes to the Chair in writing, and the Chair has 48 hours to offer a resolution.

Once the NomCom is working, anyone in the IETF community may nominate anyone, including themselves. NomCom members cannot be considered for positions the NomCom fills, and people recalled from an IESG, IAB, IETF Trust or IETF LLC Board position in the previous two years are ineligible. A nominee must consent in writing before becoming a candidate, and the NomCom presents confirming bodies with testimony about each candidate. Rejected nominees and candidates must be told before confirmed candidates are announced.
sections.eli5: Names go into a hat and are drawn in a way anyone can check. No company gets more than two seats. Then anyone can suggest who should get each job, as long as that person says they are willing.

sections.title: Voting, Quorum and Disputes
sections.content:
The Chair must establish a voting mechanism and criteria for closure that every member knows. For a candidate selection vote, a quorum is at least seven of the voting volunteers. For other votes, a quorum is at least 75% of the NomCom members participating. Rules not otherwise specified are at the committee's discretion. A member other than the Chair may be recalled from the NomCom if at least a quorum of all members agree, and only the prior year's Chair may request the recall of the current Chair. If one voting seat is vacated, the committee may proceed with nine voting volunteers.

When a process problem cannot be settled inside the committee, the dispute resolution process applies. A written request goes to the Internet Society President, who appoints an arbiter (self-appointment is permitted). The arbiter investigates, decides after consulting the two principal parties, and reports. The result is final and binding with no appeal, the NomCom must not submit any candidates to a confirming body until the issue is resolved, and the process should finish within two weeks.
sections.eli5: The group needs enough people present before any vote counts. If they cannot agree about the rules, a neutral referee decides, and everyone has to accept it.

sections.title: Recalling a Sitting Leader
sections.content:
The recall process applies to IESG and IAB members, NomCom-appointed IETF Trust Trustees and NomCom-appointed IETF LLC Directors. A signed petition goes to the Internet Society President. There are two kinds. A community petition needs at least 20 members of the IETF community who qualify as NomCom voting members, with no more than two signatories sharing a primary affiliation, and must include a justification and supporting documents. An Ombudsteam petition follows RFC 7776 and needs no community signatures.

The Internet Society President appoints a Recall Committee Chair but must not evaluate the request, because the IETF community is responsible for judging its leaders. The recall committee is created and run like a NomCom, except that the person under investigation and the petitioners cannot be members and there is no confirmation step. It investigates, which must include a written statement from the person and consultation with third parties, then votes. A 3/4 majority of the members who vote on the question is required, and a recalled seat is filled under the mid-term vacancy rules.
sections.eli5: If enough people think a leader is doing a bad job, they can sign a request. A new group looks into it, listens to the leader, and needs a big majority to remove them.

sections.title: Security and Confidentiality
sections.content:
The security section is about information handling. Any selection, confirmation or recall process involves looking into the qualifications and activities of candidates, which may reveal confidential or private information. Everyone who takes part must keep confidential anything not explicitly identified as suitable for public release.

When the NomCom needs to share confidential information with others, the sharing must be minimal, and each person consulted must first commit to the same confidentiality rules as the NomCom. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: People checked by the committee might have private stuff come up, so everyone promises to keep it secret and only share what they truly must.
